claims.text: A thin Ni interlayer on W particles will enhance W–Cu interfacial wetting during spark plasma sintering.
A thin Ni interlayer on W particles will enhance W–Cu interfacial bonding during spark plasma sintering.
Ni interfacial modification will reduce void formation and phase separation in W–Cu composites.
Ni interfacial modification will improve thermal transport and mechanical durability under fusion-relevant irradiation relative to conventional vapor-coated W-powder processing.
W particles or interconnected W regions dispersed in a Cu matrix produced by conventional methods exhibit interfacial voids and phase separation.
The proposed intervention is to deposit a controlled thin Ni coating on W surfaces before spark plasma sintering.
Processing will occur at temperatures well below the boiling point of Cu and the melting point of W.
The intended service environment includes thermal cycling and irradiation typical of fusion-reactor joints.
The structural mediator is a nanoscale Ni interlayer at W–Cu interfaces.
The Ni coating lowers the interfacial energy between W and Cu.
Lower W–Cu interfacial energy promotes improved wetting and more uniform infiltration of Cu into a W scaffold.
Enhanced W–Cu interfacial bonding reduces void formation and phase separation.
Reduced void formation and phase separation improve the composite's thermal and mechanical properties under irradiation.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will have fewer interfacial voids than otherwise comparable composites without Ni.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will have a more continuous metal network and higher thermal conductivity than composites without Ni.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will retain better mechanical durability after fusion-relevant irradiation than composites without Ni.
